description: Hey, I am Pearlin, I am an ui/ux+frontend developer.
summary:
We built a web dashboard that pulls NASA’s published microgravity flame data from the SAFFIRE and BASS experiments into one place. It covers 75 tests, with oxygen level, airflow, fuel, thickness, spread rate, flame length and burn outcome side by side. Users can compare tests in charts, search by conditions such as oxygen and flow, and see flagged data gaps. A simple regression model fitted to the BASS-II PMMA data gives a rough what-if estimate of spread rate.

It makes scattered PSI results easier to find, compare and interpret, and it supports predictive modelling. A flammability map of thin-fabric tests shows where flames ignite, quench or blow off. It also exposes a gap: tests only reach about 27% oxygen, below the 30% or more expected for Moon bases.

Fire is one of the most dangerous risks on a spacecraft or lunar base, and designers need clear, comparable data on how fast flames spread and when they go out. The same data can inform fire safety on Earth.

Limits: all values are published NASA numbers, and the model is exploratory (held-out R² about 0.37).
details:
What it does and how it works
The dashboard collects published NASA microgravity flame data from the SAFFIRE and BASS experiments in the PSI database into one table of 75 tests. Each test records oxygen, airflow, fuel, thickness, spread rate, flame length and outcome, taken from NASA tables and reports. Users can:

  • See charts of spread rate against oxygen and airflow.
  • View a map of which thin-fabric tests ignited, quenched or blew off.
  • Search by conditions, with the closest matches first.
  • Try a what-if estimator, a simple regression fitted to 39 BASS-II points. It has a held-out R² of about 0.37, so it is a rough guide.

Every value is published NASA data. Missing values are shown as blank, never as zero, and items we could not verify are listed on a “still to check” page.

Benefits
Researchers and students can find, compare and interpret fire data in minutes instead of reading many separate reports. It shows which conditions are safest, where the data is thin, and what to test next.


Faster, clearer fire-safety insight for spacecraft and habitats. It also exposes a gap: the tests reach about 27% oxygen, below the 30% or more expected for lunar bases.

Tools

  • AI: ChatGPT, Claude and SciSpace.
  • Data: NASA PSI and NASA reports.

The project is creative in how it turns scattered tables into something people can explore. It includes a flammability map of which thin-fabric tests ignited, quenched or blew off, a closest-match search instead of exact filters, and a what-if estimator that reports its own error. It also flags data gaps and conflicts openly rather than hiding them.

It uses free public data and needs no paid servers or databases, and it is a single static web page that runs in the browser. It needs only a browser and no login, with plain-language captions, labelled inputs and charts, and it works on phones.
